blocks.text: **Shares** are small equal slices of a company's capital. When a company goes public for the first time and lists on the stock exchanges to raise money from the market, investors buy one or more shares. Buying shares makes you a **part owner** of the company, in proportion to the percentage of shares you hold.

blocks.title: What a shareholder gets and risks
items: **Ownership** share in proportion to holding; a holding of 50 per cent or more makes a shareholder the biggest owner.
**Dividends** from profits; they can be paid only if the company earns profits. Otherwise the shareholder can trade the shares in the stock market to realise value.
**Risk**: owners stand to lose if the company falls into debt or goes into liquidation, because shareholders are paid out **last**.

blocks.title: Owners come last
blocks.text: Shareholders are **owners** of the company. In liquidation, outside creditors (banks, debenture holders and others) are paid first; shareholders, whatever their contribution, are paid last.

blocks.title: Who gets paid first?
blocks.phrase: Creditors Pay Early: Creditors, then Preference shareholders, then Equity shareholders.
letters: Creditors (banks, debenture holders and others) are repaid first
Preference shareholders come next in liquidation
blocks.note: The higher the risk, the later you are paid and the more voting power you usually get.

blocks.title: Equity versus preference shares
rows: Traded on the stock exchange; the most common type
Entitled to dividends; amount varies with profits
Fixed dividend, paid ahead of equity shareholders
Convertible preference shares can be converted into equity shares later

blocks.text: The no-voting limitation applies only to preference shares issued by **public companies** or private companies that have a public subsidiary. A private company can, through its **articles of association**, issue preference shares carrying similar voting rights.

blocks.title: Handy share terms
rows: Holders can claim **arrears of dividend** from future profits.
Unpaid dividend for a year is not carried forward.
Holder shares in **surplus profits** beyond the fixed dividend.
Does **not** carry the right to share in surplus profits.
Issued to employees or directors for know-how or intellectual property rights.
Shares offered to select investors; the company does **not invite the public**.
Issue of shares at a price lower than their face value.

blocks.title: Equity versus preference
blocks.phrase: Equity = Everything at risk, Entitled to vote. Preference = Priority pay, but Poor voice (no vote).
letters: Voting rights, variable dividend, paid last
Fixed dividend, priority in dividend and liquidation, no vote usually

blocks.title: Redeemable equity
blocks.text: A company **cannot** issue redeemable equity shares. It can issue redeemable preference shares and redeemable debentures.

**Debentures** are long-term **debt instruments** that a company issues under its seal. They are **borrowed capital**: like a loan from the debenture holders, to be repaid with interest in due time. Holders are paid interest at regular intervals.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Debenture holders are **creditors** of the company, not owners, and rank above shareholders.
Interest is paid **over and above profits**, so it is paid even when the company runs at a loss.
In liquidation, creditors including banks and debenture holders are repaid first; shareholders last.
Debenture holders have **no voting rights**: the main feature that tells debentures apart from shares.

blocks.title: Debenture = Debt
blocks.phrase: DEBenture = DEBt = DEBtor company owes you; you are a Creditor, not an owner.
letters: Owned fund; holder is an owner; gets dividend
Borrowed fund; holder is a creditor; gets interest

blocks.title: Five pairs of debentures
rows: **Registered**: recorded with the company, transferred by a transfer deed
**Bearer**: no record in company registers, transferred by mere delivery
**Secured**: carry a charge on the company's assets; holders can recover principal and unpaid interest from the mortgaged assets
**Redeemable**: principal repaid after a fixed time
**Non-redeemable**: repaid only on liquidation, not in the company's lifetime
**Convertible**: can be converted into shares on pre-decided terms

blocks.title: Five debenture pairs
blocks.phrase: Rich Secure Retirees Find Capital: Registered, Secured, Redeemable, First, Convertible.
blocks.note: Bearer debentures move by delivery; registered ones need a transfer deed.

blocks.title: From authorised to paid-up
rows: The **maximum** amount of capital a company can issue; it can be increased from time to time.
The part of authorised capital that is **offered to investors**.
The part of issued capital that investors have **accepted and agreed** to take.
The part of subscribed capital that investors have **actually paid**; the money truly invested in the business.

blocks.title: Capital ladder
blocks.phrase: All Investors Should Pay: Authorised, Issued, Subscribed, Paid-up.
blocks.note: Usually companies take full payment in one go, so issued, subscribed and paid-up capital often become the same.

blocks.title: Balance sheet check
blocks.text: Authorised, issued, subscribed and paid-up capital are shown under share capital. **Reserve capital** is not shown under the 'Share Capital' heading.

blocks.title: Key differences
rows: Dividend is an appropriation of profit, not a deduction
Interest is a business expense, allowed as a deduction from profit
Interest even if there is no profit
Priority over shares; repaid before them

blocks.title: One-line contrast
blocks.text: Shares: owners, dividend, voting, repaid last. Debentures: creditors, interest, no voting, repaid first.

An **Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF)** is a collection of investments such as equities or bonds that trades on an exchange like a share. It combines the **diversification of mutual funds** with the **ease of trading equities**, lets you invest in many securities at once, and often has lower fees than other funds.

blocks.title: Related terms
rows: Calculated daily; the price at which mutual fund units are bought (new purchases) and sold (redemptions), including exchanges between schemes of the same fund family.
A company's share of business volume compared with other companies.
Debt ETF with fixed maturity options of **3 years and 10 years**, as asked in an exam.

blocks.title: Do not mix these up
blocks.text: Market share is about **business volume**, not the share price quoted in the market, paid-up capital or the Sensex.

revision: Shares are small units of a company's capital; shareholders are part owners with voting rights and dividends.
In liquidation, creditors are repaid first, then preference shareholders, then equity shareholders last.
Equity shares are the ordinary shares traded on exchanges; they carry voting rights.
Preference shares carry a fixed dividend and priority over equity, but generally no voting rights.
Convertible preference shares can be converted into equity shares later.
Cumulative preference shares carry the right to arrears of dividend; non-participating ones do not share surplus profits.
A company cannot issue redeemable equity shares.
Debentures are long-term debt instruments issued under the company's seal; holders are creditors, not owners.
Debenture interest is payable even without profit and is a business expense; dividend is paid only from profit.
Debenture holders have no voting rights.
Debenture pairs: registered/bearer, secured/unsecured, redeemable/non-redeemable, first/second, convertible/non-convertible.
Bearer debentures transfer by delivery; registered ones by a transfer deed.
Share capital order: authorised, issued, subscribed, paid-up; authorised capital is the maximum and can be raised.
Sweat equity shares go to employees or directors for know-how or IPR; issue below face value is an issue at a discount.
ETFs combine mutual fund diversification with the ease of trading equities; NAV is the price for mutual fund transactions.
